sources.title: Canon TDD (Kent Beck)
sources.publisher: Kent Beck, Software Design: Tidy First?
findings: Steps: write a test list of behavior variants, turn exactly one item into a concrete automated test, make it pass, optionally refactor, repeat until the list is empty.
Named mistakes: tests without assertions written for coverage; converting the whole test list into tests up front; mixing implementation design into the test list.
sources.limits: Practitioner definition by the originator of TDD; no controlled study.

sources.title: Test Desiderata (Kent Beck)
findings: Twelve properties that make tests valuable, among them isolated, composable, deterministic, fast, behavioral (sensitive to behavior changes), structure-insensitive (unchanged by structure changes), specific (cause of failure obvious), and predictive.
Properties trade off against each other; composability can make tests faster and more predictive at once.
sources.limits: Property list read on the page; the linked videos not watched.

sources.title: Behavior Change = Revenue Versus Structure Change = Option (Kent Beck)
sources.publisher: Kent Beck, Software Design: Tidy First?
findings: A change alters either the system's behavior or its structure; Beck suggests never changing both at the same time.
Behavior changes earn now and can reduce optionality; structure changes should always increase optionality and earn nothing directly.
sources.limits: Essay from the Tidy First? series; the book itself not read for this entry.

sources.title: Definition Of Refactoring (Martin Fowler)
findings: Refactoring: a change to the internal structure of software that makes it easier to understand and cheaper to modify without changing its observable behavior.

sources.title: Catalog of Refactorings (Martin Fowler)
findings: Online catalog of the named refactorings from Refactoring, 2nd edition (for example Extract Function, Rename Variable, Split Phase), tagged by kind.
sources.limits: Catalog names read; the mechanics of each entry are in the book.

sources.title: An example of preparatory refactoring (Martin Fowler)
findings: Preparatory refactoring, after Kent Beck: for each desired change, make the change easy (which may be hard), then make the easy change.

sources.title: Yagni (Martin Fowler)
findings: A presumptive feature built before it is needed carries a cost of delay and a cost of carry even when the guess is right.
Citing Kohavi et al., only about one third of carefully analyzed features improved the metric they targeted, so a presumptive feature is more likely wrong than right.
sources.limits: Yagni does not apply to effort that makes the code easier to change, such as refactoring.

sources.title: Code Smell (Martin Fowler)
findings: A code smell is a surface indication, quick to spot, that usually corresponds to a deeper problem; a smell is not always a problem.
sources.limits: Short bliki entry; the smell catalog is in the Refactoring book.

sources.title: Beck Design Rules (Martin Fowler)
findings: Kent Beck's four rules of simple design, in priority order: passes the tests, reveals intention, no duplication, fewest elements.
sources.limits: Fowler's phrasing; Beck's own formulation is in Extreme Programming Explained.

sources.title: A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd edition (John Ousterhout)
findings: Second edition (July 2021) adds the chapter Decide What Matters, expands General-Purpose Modules are Deeper, and compares the book with Clean Code, disagreeing on method length and the role of comments.
sources.limits: Book page read; deep modules, pass-through methods, and comments that describe what is not obvious are from the book's chapters, not the page.

sources.title: Flag Argument (Martin Fowler)
findings: A flag argument tells a function to carry out a different operation depending on its value; prefer separate, explicitly named functions, keeping any flagged implementation private.

sources.title: Parallel Change (Danilo Sato)
findings: Parallel change (expand and contract) splits a backward-incompatible interface change into expand, migrate, and contract, so consumers keep working during the move.

sources.title: Test Double (Martin Fowler)
findings: Test double is the generic term for a stand-in for a production object; Meszaros's kinds are dummy, fake, stub, spy, and mock.
sources.limits: Vocabulary entry; trade-offs in Mocks Aren't Stubs.

sources.title: Mocks Aren't Stubs (Martin Fowler)
findings: Distinguishes state verification from behavior verification and classical from mockist TDD; a classicist uses real objects for easy collaborations and a double only for awkward ones.

sources.title: Given When Then (Martin Fowler)
findings: Given-When-Then, from Dan North and Chris Matts in Behavior-Driven Development, specifies a behavior as the state before, the behavior under test, and the expected changes.
